```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(RdistNN)
```

The order `s` controls localization: larger values concentrate weight closer
to the reporting profile. A grid compares estimates across orders and retains
its specified default; it does not select an optimal order. The
[paper](https://jakobjuergens.com/research/#orthogonal-inference-conditional-z)
gives the statistical motivation and inference conditions.

## Fit and compare a grid

```{r wrapper-integration}
demo <- np_demo_data(n = 200, p = 2, seed = 1)
fit <- np_dnn(
  data = demo$data, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y",
  x0 = demo$x0, tuning_mode = "grid"
)
fit$tuning_grid$candidates
fit$tuning_grid$estimates
```

The main estimate remains the default candidate. Use a candidate view to
inspect another order without fitting the nuisance functions again:

```{r candidate}
view <- candidate_fit(fit, 1L)
coef(view)
```

Candidate identifiers refer to rows of the tuning grid, not just the resolved
order. If two tuning settings resolve to the same `s`, they remain distinct
candidates even when their computation is shared. Plot labels include their
identifiers when needed to distinguish them. Candidate reconstruction validates
the retained controls, target identities, cached ranks, per-target distance
groups and selected policy; refit an incomplete
or inconsistent saved object.

CATE and CLATE use the same `tuning_mode` convention. See
[Getting started](getting-started.html) and [Conditional LATE](conditional-late.html)
for their signal inputs. `plot_tuning(fit)` draws the sensitivity comparison
when ggplot2 is installed.

## Inspect the default rule

The built-in rule is `floor(lambda * n^((kx + 1)/(kx + 2)))`, with
`lambda = 0.4` and sensitivity multipliers `c(0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.75)`.
Here `kx` is the number of reporting covariates. `lambda = 1` remains an
available, more concentrated localization setting. Delete-one uncertainty
requires `s < n`.

```{r paper-default}
tun <- tuning_dnn_paper()
tuning_eval(tun, n = 1000, kx = 2, k = 1)$s
tuning_eval(tun, n = 1000, kx = 2, k = 1, mode = "grid")$candidates
```

Explicit `s` and a tuning specification are alternative inputs; grid mode
cannot be combined with explicit `s`. Diagnostics record the resolved order
and its provenance:

```{r metadata}
as.data.frame(diagnostics(fit))[, c("target_id", "tuning_name", "tuning_default_s")]
```

## Define and register a custom rule

For a fixed order, a small function is enough:

```{r custom}
fixed12 <- as_tuning(function(...) 12L, name = "fixed_12")
tuning_eval(fixed12, n = 300, kx = 2, k = 1)$s
register_tuning("fixed_12", fixed12)
get_tuning("fixed_12")$name
```

`new_tuning()` also accepts explicit candidate generation and metadata; see
its help for the full interface. A custom rule must respect the estimator's
order constraints. [DNN weights](dnn-weights.html) explains the resulting
rank weights, and [Notation and conventions](notation-and-conventions.html)
lists the argument and result shapes.
